### Problem: Minimum Split Into Subarrays With GCD Greater Than One {#sec-gcd-p2-split}

::: {.p-statement}
**Cut the array so every piece has a shared factor.** Given an integer array `nums`, split
it into the **minimum number of contiguous subarrays** so that the greatest common divisor
of each subarray is **greater than 1**. A subarray of one element has gcd equal to that
element.

```text
nums = [12, 6, 3, 14, 8]  -> 2      (subarrays [12, 6, 3] with gcd 3, and [14, 8] with gcd 2)
nums = [4, 12, 6, 14]     -> 1      (the whole array has gcd 2)
```

**Constraints.** $1 \le n \le 2000$; $2 \le \mathit{nums}[i] \le 10^9$.
Source: [LC 2436 · Minimum Split Into Subarrays With GCD Greater Than One](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-split-into-subarrays-with-gcd-greater-than-one/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
The running gcd of a segment is **monotone**: extending a segment can only shrink the gcd
or leave it, never grow it. So greedy wins here - keep the current segment open as long as
the running gcd stays above 1, and the moment adding the next element would drop it to 1,
you are *forced* to cut. Any valid split must also cut there, because no segment spanning
that point can have gcd $> 1$. Since every value is at least $2$, a split always exists -
in the worst case every element stands alone - so there is no impossible case to handle.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Greedily extend, cut when forced.** Fold a running gcd; each time the next element
   would send it to 1, start a new segment. This is the answer directly.
2. **See it as forced cuts.** The count is one plus the number of positions where the
   running segment gcd collapses to 1 - which is exactly a fold that resets at each
   collapse, and it makes the "cut is forced" argument a one-line proof.
:::

::: {#fig-gcd-p2-split}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    V.grid(ax, p, [["index", "0", "1", "2", "3", "4"],
                   ["value", "12", "6", "3", "14", "8"],
                   ["segment", "S0", "S0", "S0", "S1", "S1"]],
           colors={(2, 4): "amber"}, cell_w=0.95)
V.show(draw)
```

The greedy run keeps $12, 6, 3$ open ($\gcd(12, 6) = 6$, $\gcd(6, 3) = 3$, both above $1$)
and cuts before $14$ ($\gcd(3, 14) = 1$), leaving two segments whose gcds are $3$ and
$2$ - the statement's own Example 1. The amber cell is the forced cut point.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Greedy running gcd, cut when it reaches 1

::: {.form-next}
Carry `g = gcd` of the current open segment. For each new element, if $\gcd(g, x) > 1$ keep
the segment and update `g`; otherwise cut - start a fresh segment at `x`. The number of
segments is the answer.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("split", "greedy")
    assert str(final) == "2"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def sp_greedy(nums):
    seg, g = 1, nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        ng = math.gcd(g, x)
        if ng > 1:
            g = ng
        else:
            seg += 1
            g = x
    return seg

assert sp_greedy([12, 6, 3, 14, 8]) == 2
assert sp_greedy([4, 12, 6, 14]) == 1
assert sp_greedy([2, 3, 5, 7]) == 4
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long mygcd(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b) { long long t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

int spGreedy(vector<int>& nums) {
    int seg = 1;
    long long g = nums[0];
    for (size_t i = 1; i < nums.size(); ++i) {
        long long ng = mygcd(g, nums[i]);
        if (ng > 1) g = ng;
        else { ++seg; g = nums[i]; }
    }
    return seg;
}
```

:::

#### One plus the forced cuts

::: {.form-next}
Reframe the same scan: every position where the running segment gcd first reaches 1 is a
boundary you cannot avoid, so the answer is one more than those positions. Reading several
arrays side by side is how you internalise the rule.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("split", "probe")
    assert str(final) == "1"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def sp_cuts(nums):
    cuts, g = 0, nums[0]
    for x in nums[1:]:
        g = math.gcd(g, x)          # fold first, then read whether it collapsed
        if g == 1:
            cuts += 1
            g = x
    return cuts + 1

# the greedy fold and the forced-cut reading are the same machine:
for arr in ([12, 6, 3, 14, 8], [4, 12, 6, 14], [2, 3, 5, 7], [2, 4, 6, 8]):
    assert sp_cuts(arr) == sp_greedy(arr)
assert sp_cuts([2, 3, 4, 6]) == 3
```

##### C++

```cpp
long long mygcd(long long a, long long b) {
    while (b) { long long t = a % b; a = b; b = t; }
    return a;
}

int spCuts(vector<int>& nums) {
    int cuts = 0;
    long long g = nums[0];
    for (size_t i = 1; i < nums.size(); ++i) {
        g = mygcd(g, nums[i]);
        if (g == 1) { ++cuts; g = nums[i]; }
    }
    return cuts + 1;
}
```

:::

:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Time.** $O(n \log V)$ - one pass, a gcd per element, $V \le 10^9$. **Space.** $O(1)$.
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- **Single element.** `nums = [5]` has gcd 5 > 1, so the answer is 1.
- **Whole array already valid.** Every element even gives one segment regardless of length.
- **Adjacent forced cuts.** `[2, 3, 5]` cuts twice (three singletons) because every pair
  of distinct primes is coprime.

**Debug tip.** If a segment of length 1 whose value is prime is being merged into its
neighbour, your gcd test is `>= 1` instead of `> 1` - every gcd is at least 1, so that
condition never cuts.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- Resetting the running gcd to $0$ (or leaving the old value in place) after a cut, instead
  of seeding the new segment with the element that triggered the cut - every later gcd is
  then measured against the wrong open segment.
- Trying to make segments *equal* in length. The objective is the count of segments, not a
  balanced partition; greedily maximising each segment is optimal because gcd is monotone.
:::

**Variants.** @sec-gcd-p1-arrgcd folds the gcd over the whole array; here the same fold
runs per segment and the *cut points* are the answer. @sec-gcd-p3-subseq asks what gcd
values are reachable at all - the fold, but over subsequences.
